header:
Date: 2027-03-02
Time: 16:23 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Rina Patel (Redwood CSM), Priya Rao (CTO, Cascade AI), Evan Kim (Lead ML Infra), Sofia Martinez (SRE), Aaron Li (ML Engineer)
summary: Technical deep-dive focused on tail latency (p95/p99) for Cascade AI's real-time assistant workload. Covered batch vs streaming behavior, KV cache hit patterns, quantization tradeoffs, networking/VPC hops, and on-prem constraints. Agreed to run additional benchmarks with representative traffic and share traces.
topics: KV cache prefix hit-rate and shard locality
network hops, VPC peering and cross-AZ traffic
transcript:
00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving out time. we have about an hour, is that still good?
00:08 Priya Rao: Yes that's perfect, thanks Maya. main thing for us is p99 - our customers are seeing jitter around 300 to 900ms spikes and we need root cause.
00:16 Liam O'Neill: Cool, can you give a quick runbook of the workload? tokens, streaming or non-streaming, model size?
00:22 Aaron Li: Sure - it's mostly real-time assistant, median response length ~80 tokens, 1.2k tokens max, mix of short prompts and some long context. we use streaming in prod for UI.
00:34 Sofia Martinez: And infra - currently on GCP with a private VPC, we have service-to-service over a peered VPC to the model endpoints. latency across regions is minimal but cross-az sometimes spikes.
00:45 Liam O'Neill: Got it. quick note: when you say spikes are 300-900ms, is that overall end-to-end or just token generation?
00:51 Priya Rao: End-to-end, so network + model. our instrumentation splits it but it's a bit fuzzy.
00:58 Liam O'Neill: okay, so typical sources: runtime scheduling (batching), KV cache misses causing full decode, quantization overhead or dynamic fallback, and network hops. we'll walk through each.
01:08 Maya Chen: Also want to mention — Redwood Dedicated vs Redwood hosted, sometimes names get munged in logs, but the runtime differences are mainly about pinning capacity and avoiding noisy-neighbor batching variance.
01:21 Evan Kim: We actually ran a quick compare with Vertex and saw slightly better median on Redwood but tails were similar, so we're trying to understand the micro-behavior.
01:30 Liam O'Neill: Perfect — first thing p95/p99 measurement. Are you sampling traces at request ingress, model start, and final token?
01:38 Aaron Li: We have timestamps at client send, gateway receive, model start, model end, and client render. sometimes the model start timestamp is missing or wrong.
01:47 Liam O'Neill: That explains some of the instrumentation gaps, if model-start is missing you can't isolate runtime queueing versus network. recommend adding fine-grained spans.
01:56 Priya Rao: For the model, we're using a 20B LLM quantized to int8 with a custom kernel. we saw improved throughput but tail worse under bursts.
02:05 Liam O'Neill: That's common. quantization helps median but can increase variability if the kernel falls back to 16-bit paths or if cache alignment differs. any fallback logs?
02:15 Aaron Li: We do see occasional 'kernel fallback' logs but they're not well correlated with spikes.
02:22 Liam O'Neill: okay, next KV cache. are you using prefix caching across requests and is it sharded by customer or by model?
02:29 Evan Kim: KV cache is sharded per-instance and we do a per-customer key namespace. sometimes cache misses happen when requests route to different GPUs.
02:37 Liam O'Neill: There you go — cross-shard routing causes cold-cache p99s. Redwood's KV cache model typically keeps hot prefixes local and will route by affinity; without affinity, you see p99 spikes when you miss the local KV.
02:49 Priya Rao: How do you measure cache hit ratio at tail?
02:53 Liam O'Neill: We recommend measuring by per-request prefix length and cache hit boolean and then compute hit-rate conditioned on the tail bucket samples. For streaming, misses early in token stream cost more because every token gets uncached decode.
03:05 Sofia Martinez: About streaming vs non-streaming - we think streaming is adding overhead because of the extra churn on the socket.
03:12 Liam O'Neill: Streaming itself is typically cheaper overall for perceived latency, but it introduces per-token small writes and flushes. If you have many tiny tokens, context switching and Nagle/tcp settings can add jitter. also server-side batching for streaming is harder because you can't wait too long to flush.
03:27 Aaron Li: So non-streaming gives better p99?
03:30 Liam O'Neill: Not necessarily. Non-streaming hides token-by-token jitter at the cost of increased tail when queuing is high. For p99 specifically, batching policies matter: if you set a max-wait of 8ms for batching you'll absorb bursts; if you set 0ms you get lower median but worse tail under load.
03:46 Maya Chen: just to add, Redwood runtime supports adaptive batching where it respects latency SLOs and will throttle batch windows to hit p95 targets while allowing p99 to be a bit higher — we can tune that per-route.
03:58 Priya Rao: Can you walk through a concrete scenario - say 50 concurrent users with 200ms SLO, what happens?
04:05 Liam O'Neill: Sure. short version: incoming requests go to a frontend layer -> routing -> model-serving pool. routing decides affinity (prefer same GPU for cache hits). if cache hit and small tokens, you'll stream with sub-100ms model latency; if cache miss and batch forms, model decode might be 60-150ms depending on seq length. network hops add 10-60ms depending on cross-az. tails happen when multiple factors align: cross-shard routes, large seq, and kernel fallback.
04:31 Evan Kim: On our topology we have a NAT and an extra hop because of peering — that could be 20-30ms.
04:36 Liam O'Neill: Yep that matters for p99. Also TLS termination location and whether the model is in a different AZ can add variance.
04:43 Priya Rao: What about quantization — does int4 help tails?
04:47 Liam O'Neill: int4 often reduces median and token CPU time, but quality regressions can force CPU-side post-processing or re-run which kills tails. int8 is usually safest; mixed-precision kernels can sometimes fallback if not aligned which causes big spikes.
05:01 Aaron Li: Any recommendations for on-prem or VPC deployments? we might consider private for compliance.
05:06 Liam O'Neill: On-prem introduces network determinism benefits but you still need pinned capacity to avoid queueing variance. Redwood Private can be deployed in-customer VPC with local model pools to keep KV cache hot. key is to minimize cross rack/host memcopy for KV cache.
05:20 Sofia Martinez: What about batching policies — how granular can we set them?
05:24 Liam O'Neill: You can set per-route max-batch-size, max-wait-ms, and a priority for streaming vs non-streaming. we also have predictive batching that uses moving-average arrival rates to decide. For p99 tuning, we often recommend slightly smaller max-batch and a short max-wait to limit tail amplification from large requests.
05:40 Priya Rao: Can you explain tail amplification?
05:42 Liam O'Neill: Sure — if a big request is in a batch, it slows that whole batch; smaller requests in the same batch inherit that latency. So tails get amplified whenever batching isn't size-aware. Redwood has size-aware batching to mitigate this.
05:56 Maya Chen: quick interjection — sometimes logs label things 'redwood dedicate' or 'redwood private' which confuses customers, we should send the canonical naming.
06:03 Rina Patel: We'll include a docs link in the follow-up.
06:07 Evan Kim: On instrumentation, you recommended adding model-start spans; can you give exact places to instrument?
06:12 Liam O'Neill: Instrument at ingress, post-auth, pre-routing, model-queue-enter, model-start, model-end, and network-egress. that gives you queueing vs execution split.
06:21 Aaron Li: For our tests, we can share a 1k-sample trace set, is that enough?
06:25 Liam O'Neill: Good start. for p99 you want at least 5k-10k samples to get stable estimates but 1k with focus on tail buckets is useful.
06:33 Priya Rao: We saw one case where the GPU kernel fallback correlated with a particular batch-size. any guidance on kernel selection?
06:39 Liam O'Neill: Kernel selection is heuristics: sequence length, head count, quantization. runtime will pick an optimized kernel for common lengths; if your seq distribution has long tails it may pick a slow path occasionally. recommend aligning model config (max_seq) with your observed distribution and enabling optimized-kernel prewarming.
06:57 Sofia Martinez: Prewarming — is that a warm start or a persistent kernel cache?
07:00 Liam O'Neill: It's both. we keep warmed kernels and pre-allocated scratch memory for common shapes, reducing first-request jitter.
07:07 Maya Chen: let's talk numbers — what p99 reductions have customers seen with affinity + KV-locality improvements?
07:13 Liam O'Neill: We often see p99 drop from 900ms to ~220-300ms in similar workloads by improving routing affinity and enabling size-aware batching and prewarmed kernels. median may not change much but tails tighten a lot.
07:25 Priya Rao: That would be great. are there any quick wins we can do while full benchmarking runs happen?
07:29 Liam O'Neill: Quick wins: increase routing affinity TTL, enable size-aware batching, set conservative max-wait-ms for critical routes, and ensure TLS termination is colocated. also tune tcp nodelay and socket buffers for streaming.
07:41 Evan Kim: For the benchmarking, can you run both streaming and non-streaming with identical request traces? we want apples-to-apples.
07:46 Liam O'Neill: Absolutely — we can replay the same trace in both modes and produce p50/p95/p99 plus per-token latency distribution.
07:52 Maya Chen: also include KV-cache hit-conditioned tail. that's crucial.
07:56 Aaron Li: Any gotchas with observability? our current exporter rolls up percentiles at 1m buckets which hides spikes.
08:03 Liam O'Neill: Yes, roll-up hides. we recommend using raw trace sampling for tail and store histograms at 10s or even 1s granularity for p99.
08:10 Priya Rao: Security questions — if we go Redwood Private in our VPC, how is key management handled?
08:15 Maya Chen: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS, HSM integrations and audit logs. we'll send the SOC2 and ISO docs.
08:22 Priya Rao: Great. any SLA impacts on these tail-tuning recommendations?
08:26 Rina Patel: Our Dedicated and Private offerings have SLA tiers; tuning is orthogonal but reserved capacity reduces noisy neighbor variance which helps tails.
08:33 Sofia Martinez: One more — what about training vs serving interference on the same infra?
08:37 Liam O'Neill: Avoid co-locating heavy training on serving nodes. it's predictable: background training causes queue increases and kernel eviction. keep serving pools isolated or schedule training off hours.
08:46 Priya Rao: ok makes sense. can you list what you'll include in the benchmark package?
08:50 Liam O'Neill: We'll include: raw p50/p95/p99 per-route, per-token breakdown, kernel fallback logs correlated with sample ids, KV-cache hit/miss tagging, and a replay script.
09:00 Maya Chen: Recap — Redwood to run benchmark replay (streaming and non-streaming), send security docs, customer to send topology + traces, follow-up in two weeks. any final questions?
09:10 Priya Rao: No, this was super useful. thanks.
09:13 Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and invite for the follow-up.
09:18 (call ends)
